editorial.headline: Marine Ornamentals, Open at National Scale and Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This code covers non-protected marine ornamental fish culture, from nursery and breeding through harvest, with foreign ownership open nationally and no Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
Marine ornamental fish culture under this activity is not a vague aquarium-trade label. It is the practical aquaculture work around non-protected saltwater ornamental species: nursery, maintenance, grow-out, breeding or hatchery activity, and harvest. The record names seahorses, clownfish, angel piyama, and blue devil as examples, and it anchors the activity in saltwater cultivation rather than capture or retail. The place can vary: open sea, river mouths, lagoons, artificial facilities, or any other site where seawater is the cultivation medium.

That scope matters because the code is built for operators whose business is the biological production of marine ornamental fish, not simply handling them after the fact. A founder registering this activity should be able to point to the cultivation chain itself: juveniles being nursed, fish being maintained and grown, broodstock or seed activity being managed, and harvest forming part of the operating cycle. The record keeps the category broad enough for different production environments, but the centre of gravity is clear: this is organised saltwater aquaculture for ornamental species that are not protected.

The access picture is unusually clean. Nationally, the activity is marked open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. It is also open across the full business-size range stated in the record: micro, small, medium, and large. That combination makes the code structurally accessible rather than reserved for only one operating size. A small specialist hatchery, a medium aquaculture operator, or a larger marine-culture project all sit within the scale language supplied by the record, provided the activity remains the cultivation of non-protected marine ornamental fish.

Bali does not change that conclusion into a hidden block. The provincial moratorium described in the record blocks all low and medium-low risk KBLI for PMA across the island, but this activity is not blocked on the Bali record supplied here. The stated reason is that OSS risk at large scale is medium-high or high, so it falls outside the moratorium block. The honest reading is therefore straightforward: for this activity, a foreign-owned company is nationally open up to 100%, and Bali is not marked as blocked by the moratorium in the slim record.
